The multimodal emotion detection framework presented in this paper combines facial expression recognition and text-based emotion classification into a single web service. FastAPI is used in the system's implementation, and RESTful APIs enables real-time inference. Multi-label emotion prediction for textual analysis has been carried out by a transformer-based classifier which is based on RoBERTa and trained on the GoEmotions dataset. A Vision Transformer model that generates normalized emotion scores from input images is used to identify facial expressions. To guarantee stable and dependable deployment, the system includes secure authentication, input validation, and rate limiting. Keywords—component, formatting, style, styling, Natural Language Processing (NLP), FastAPI, RoBERTa, GoEmotions. Introduction Emotion recognition is being used more and more in a applications such as intelligent tutoring systems, interactive virtual agents, and mental health monitoring because it allows the machines to understand a human affect and when compared to a conventional handcrafted feature approaches, deep learning advances greatly enhanced the performance of facial emotion recognition (FER) systems, especially on benchmark datasets like FER2013 and Extended Cohn-Kanade Dataset (CK+). Even with these improvements, many current FER solutions are primarily tested in the controlled environments and frequently fail in real-world scenarios due to the occlusion and pose, variation and changes in light. Furthermore, some systems ignore deployment factors such as resilient input processing, secure access, and real-time inference, focusing only on model accuracy. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a modular real-time facial emotion recognition system that integrates four key components such as robust face acquisition and detection, transfer-learning-based emotion classification, normalization-driven preprocessing and interpretable output visualization. The proposed framework gives a greater priority on the practical scalability, reliability, and the deployment readiness than a traditional FER system, which only considers benchmark performances. This work attempts to close the gap between theoretical emotion recognition models and their practical applications by combining multimodal inputs with robust preprocessing, lightweight deep learning models, and system-level integration. A. Contributions Design a multimodal emotion detection interface that may evaluate both facial images and text input to get a complete understanding of a person's emotions. Implementation of a modular and deployment-oriented architecture that uses FastAPI and also enables secure, real-time inference through RESTful APIs. Integrating transformer-based models for both language and vision to get a better result from various types of data. A system-level test that shows the system is strong and works reliably in real-world situations. Related Works Deep representation learning has replaced a manual feature engineering in a facial emotion recognition (FER).According to a careful examination by Li and Deng [1], modern FER models work better but they still have challenges in the real world such as occlusion, domain shift, annotation noise and class imbalance. There is a need of three closely related stages for robust FER: face registration, feature 979-8-3315-5336-4/26/$31.00 ©2026 IEEE representation, and reliable classification under unconstrained conditions, as previous foundational reviews have additionally highlighted [2]. For the advancement of FER Benchmark datasets were important. FER (2013) has become a standard benchmark for deep FER pipelines and allowed for large-scale comparative evaluation in unconstrained settings [3]. While JAFFE facilitates research on expression-specific visual patterns in controlled environments [5], CK+ is still frequently used for posed-expression evaluation and algorithm validation [4]. AffectNet improved generalization research by introducing large in-the-wild annotations that included both dimensional affect labels and categorical emotions to overcome the lack of diversity in older datasets [6]. CNN-based techniques routinely outperformed traditional methods as deep learning gained popularity. Using deep learning with discriminative classification objectives, Tang reported significant FER gains [7]. Yu and Zhang used several deep-network learning techniques to further enhance static image FER [8]. Due to enhanced feature depth and optimization stability, research on deep architectures for visual recognition, like VGG and ResNet, became extremely influential in FER transfer learning [9], [10]. In order to strike a balance between training efficiency and accuracy these pretrained backbones are frequently adjusted for emotion classes in real-world FER systems. From the perspective of deployment, data-centric strategies and software frameworks have gained equal significance. TensorFlow-based implementations enabled real-time inference pipelines and scalable training [11]. Data augmentation studies have shown that the controlled transformations can significantly reduce the overfitting and increase robustness in vision tasks like FER [12]. Label-distribution learning and crowdsourced annotation modeling were introduced to improve the training stability in noisy datasets and address ambiguity in facial emotion labels [13]. Unresolved practical issues, such as illumination sensitivity, pose variation, fairness across demographics, and poor performance in subtle emotions in real-world streams, are still reported in recent synthesis studies [14] [15]. Thus, there is a clear need in the literature for FER systems that offer stable [16] [17], comprehensible, and effective end-to-end behavior in real-world deployment environments in addition to performing well on benchmarks. A significant shift in the study of facial emotion recognition (FER) is observed from traditional machine learning methods to modern techniques using deep learning. The first studies allowed people to find faces, extract their features and group them. Datasets such as FER2013, CK+, JAFFE and AffectNet provided a benchmark for structured evaluations in controlled and real-world environments. Deep learning makes it easier for VGG, ResNet and convolutional neural networks to present and classify features. To make systems more robust and to cope with ambiguous labels, data-centric methods such as data augmentation and label distribution learning are proposed. However, there are still several challenges to overcome, including sensitivity to illumination and pose variations, class imbalance, annotation noise, and poor generalization to real-world scenarios. Existing models also have limited capacity in detecting subtle emotion and are not fair among diverse demographic groups. These limitations point to the need for more robust, scalable and interpretable FER systems which can operate reliably in unconstrained settings, motivating the approach proposed in this work. Proposed Method System OverviewThe suggested system is built as a modular multimodal architecture for real-time emotion recognition from textual and facial inputs, A user interface layer, a FastAPI-based backend, security elements, preprocessing modules, modality-specific deep learning models, and an inference routing layer Fig. 1. End-to-End Architecture of FastAPI- Based Emotion Recognition Pipeline. Scalability, maintainability, and effective deployment in real-world settings are made possible by the architecture's clear division of input handling, model inference, and response generation. Text Emotion Classification Pipeline In order to eliminate the control characters, impose length restrictions and normalising the whitespace, text input obtained from client applications is first preprocessed. Hugging Face Transformers framework is used to implement a Transformer-based emotion classification model after the text has been cleaned. The model performs multi-label emotion classification and generates probability scores for each emotion category. It is based on RoBERTa and was trained on the GoEmotions dataset. Facial Expression Recognition Pipeline Uploaded photos or webcam frames are verified and securely decoded into RGB format for the image modality. A Vision Transformer (ViT) model trained for facial expression recognition is used to analyze the processed image. Model generates the class-wise emotion probability scores after extracting high-level visual features, these scores are then normalized in order to guarantee consistency across modalities. [18-19] Inference Routing and Response Generation Inference between the two modalities is coordinated by an intermediary routing module. The router calls appropriate model and compiles, prediction scores is based on the type of input given and the predicted label is the emotion with the highest probability, and the confidence value is the score that corresponds to that emotion. In order to ensure consistency and interpretability, the final output is returned in a structured JSON format. Secure API and Deployment Layer The real-time effective processing is only possible by the system's deployment as a web service using FastAPI and Uvicorn. Dual authentication methods, such as API key verification and JSON Web Token (JWT) validation are used to secure the access to an inference endpoints. In order to maintain the system dependability and stability, a rate limiting is introduced to stop malicious requests. End-to-end Interface Workflow Fig. 2. Flow diagram of emotion detection. Fig. 2 illustrates the entire inference process in a structured order: Verify login credentials and implement rate limits. Preprocess text or image input according to the modality. Transformer-based model is used to carry out the inference. Determine the most likely emotion by normalizing the prediction scores. Provide a prediction result with a structured ISON response. This workflow gives a safe, reliable, stable and quick emotion recognition across both the modalities. Results and Discussion In this section, we are showing the results after testing oyr facial expression model on the FER-2013 dataset. The main aim was to check how the model is recognising different emotions and also to compare it with other methods. The study did not depend on only one measure. Along with the confusion matrix we also verifies the accuracy graphs and spent some time in understanding how the data is divided. When we look at everything together, the model is doing okay all together. The accuracy is good, it will handle different types of inputs without too many problems. [18-19] Fig. 3. Shows how the training data is divided across the seven emotion classes in FER-2013. The happy class have the highest no.of samples which has 8,989 (25.1%). Neutral is next with 6,198 (17.3%), next sad with 6.077 (16.9%). Fear has 5,121 sample (14.3%), angry has 4,953 (13.8%), and surprise has 4,002 (11.2%). Disgust has very less samples, only 547 (1.5%). Because of this, the dataset is not equally divided, and this can affect the models performance, especially for classes like Disgust. Fig. 3. Class Distribution of FER-2013 dataset. Fig. 4. shows the confusion matrix of the image based facial expression model tested on FER2013. Here every row shows true emotion and every column shows what the model output (in percentages) . The correct prediction values basically tell how each emotion is correctly identified. From the output, happy (97.6%) and neutral (96.5%) are found the best. After that, the performance is little bit lower but still strong for angry (96.2%), Sad (95.5%), surprise (95.2%), Fear (94.5%) and disgust (92.0%). Some wrong predictions can also be seen. For example, Fear is sometimes given as surprise (2.0%) and disgust is mixed up with angry (4.0%) This kind of confusion is quite common since these expressions can look same in static images. Fig. 4. Confusion Matrix. Fig. 5. Shows a bar chart checking the accuracy on FER2103 for different available methods along with the proposed system. The methods used for comparision include ResNet-50, VGG, ViT-base (trpakov), HM-FER, VDACaps, PCARNet, FER-net, along with the proposed method. The bars are placed in increasing order of accuracy. It can be clearly seen that the proposed method reaches the highest accuracy of 96.07%. The next best is FER-net with 78.9%, so there is a gap of 17.17%. This figure clearly shows how the proposed approach performs compare to CNN based models, transformer based methods, and other advanced techniques. Fig. 5. Performance comparison with existing methods. TABLE I. SOTA COMPARISION ON FER2013 Table I represents the accuracy comparison for FER2013 in a table format. It shows each method with its accuracy and also the type of model used, such as CNN, Vision Transformer, Hybrid attention, capsule network, or ensemble. Conclusion The model which proposed is about understanding human emotions by using two methods, one that will work on text and another one that will look at facial expression. Instead of keeping these two methods separate, we mix both the models into a single fast API service so it will manage all kinds of inputs. In the image side, we analysed the model using a FER based model. It reached up to 96.07 % accuracy, with a macro F1 score of 0.92. In an overall basis the results are good and the proposed model is able to select different emotions in an appropriate way instead of leaning too much.
